question: Does a pin made the way a user makes one actually keep the bytes, or is it only an accounting entry?
why_now: Milestone 3's five boxes were classified `autonomous` in the acceptance ledger, which reads as 'only measurement is missing'. It was not. Engine::materialise_pin, Engine::pin_folder and Engine::unpin had no caller outside their own tests: `cirrove pin` wrote Store::pin directly, because only the daemon holds an engine and the command line is not the daemon. So a pin reserved cache space and fetched nothing, and the first offline read still failed -- which is the whole of what pinning is for. The README said otherwise and has been corrected separately.
prediction_provenance: Derived from reading engine.rs, accounts.rs, lib.rs and manager.rs before writing any code. No exploratory run preceded this.

what_was_blocking_it.one_verb_literally: serve_managed read exactly seven bytes and compared them to b"status\n" (lib.rs:210). A second verb was impossible without a length-variable read.
what_was_blocking_it.engines_unreachable: Manager exposed only status: RwLock<Vec<AccountStatus>>. The Running entries holding the real Arc<Engine> were a local HashMap inside run(), so nothing outside that loop had an engine to ask.
what_was_blocking_it.consequence: accounts::set_pin wrote the store out of band, which is also why refuse_to_migrate_under_a_running_daemon had to exist: a pin command run against a live state directory migrated the index it was only meant to report an error about.

change: A bounded line read on the socket with `status\n` byte-identical on the wire; an engines registry on Manager written at the same two points as status; PinRequest/PinReply and client pin/unpin; Engine::apply_pin_request resolving --path in the daemon and calling materialise_pin or pin_folder; Engine::apply_unpin_request calling a new ContentCache::reclaim.

predictions.claim: A pin issued through the control socket causes provider reads that did not happen before it.
predictions.role: the whole point. A pin that fetches nothing is an accounting entry, and the provider read counter is the only thing that can tell the two apart.

predictions.claim: cirrove status then reports the pin with blocks > 0 and resident > 0, not merely a reservation.

predictions.role: discriminator on the accounting. The reservation is what stops the cache exceeding its budget, and pinned blocks are exactly the ones eviction may not take, so a reservation that is short is not recovered later.

predictions.claim: The test cannot pass against the previous code.
predictions.role: AGENTS.md requires a test offered as proof to be shown to fail without its subject.

decision_rule: P1 and P2 must hold for the pinning boxes to have any terminal-reachable evidence at all. P3 failing would be a defect to fix rather than a reason to weaken the assertion. None of this ticks a box on its own: every clause of milestones 3's boxes also asks for kernel-mount evidence, and this runs against a fixture provider.

result.P1: HOLDS. The provider read counter advances across the pin request; it did not before, because nothing fetched.
result.P2: HOLDS. Status reports blocks > 0 and resident > 0 within the wait.
result.P3: FAILED FIRST, and found a real accounting error. resident exceeded reserved by 32 bytes. Reservations were made in logical bytes while the cache stores a SHA-256 ahead of every block, so a pinned file occupied one digest per block more than it had reserved -- and because pinned blocks are protected from eviction, the shortfall lets the cache sit that far over its budget indefinitely rather than being recovered. Fixed by content::stored_bytes, used for both the single-file reservation and the folder walk. P3 then holds.
result.P4: HOLDS. Against the previous source the test does not compile: `cannot find function pin in crate cirrove_service` and `cannot find struct PinRequest`. The daemon's socket answers only the seven bytes status\n, so there is no client verb to call.

what_this_does_not_show: The fixture provider is in-process and the mount is not involved: nothing here reads a pinned file through the kernel with the provider unreachable, which is what the offline boxes actually ask for. That is the next step, not this one.
decision: The path exists for the first time. No acceptance box is ticked on this artifact.
